citation: Theodore J. Karamanski, 'Monuments to a Lost Nation', reprinted from Chicago History, Spring 2004, on the University of Illinois American Indian Online Project (chicagomem6). Read 15 November 2026.
author: Theodore J. Karamanski
locator: Page 6 of the essay, on Carl Rohl-Smith's Fort Dearborn Massacre group.
rights_note: Cited in words only; nothing copied beyond short quoted fragments.
access_notes: Read 2026-11-15 (the 1904 story jaunts) from the page's own text, fetched whole; this record is cited only for what that text says.
note: Rohl-Smith obtained his models at Fort Sheridan, where he met survivors of Wounded Knee, 'Indians of the most untamed sort'; 'a year after the statue's dedication', the Seventh Cavalry, 'which had fought Indians so fiercely at Little Big Horn and Wounded Knee, came to Chicago to quell the Pullman riots of 1894'; 'Some historians regard the incident as the product of romantic imagination instead of eyewitness testimony, stating that Margaret Helm was not the beneficiary of Black Partridge's dramatic rescue. In fact, before the battle turned into a massacre, Mrs. Helm rode her horse to the shore of Lake Michigan where she found refuge.' The figures 'may have owed more to Buffalo Bill Cody's Wild West Show than to actual research.'
what_it_supplies: the historians' doubt about the rescue the bronze shows
what_it_does_not_supply: the statue's later moves (the essay's later page, karamanski_2004_monuments_lost_nation)
